title: Ember AI — Migration & eval parity discovery
transcript:
Header: 2025-06-18 15:00 UTC | Duration ~46 min | Recording: Zoom
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Samir (CTO, Ember), Maya (Head of ML), Dan (Infra), Jules (PM)
Links shared: Redwood migration deck (link), eval spreadsheet (link), security pack (link)

Summary: quick discovery focused on migration from OpenAI-hosted pipelines and a self-hosted vLLM/TGI setup. Customer is looking for parity on quality and tighter cost predictability; they flagged KMS, VPC, and a short POC with eval prompts. Transcript follows (auto transcribed, medium quality; occasional mis-hearings).

[00:00] Alex: hey everyone thanks for making the time, um quick intro from our side, I'm Alex, I run the AE for this region, Priya is our lead SE on inference and Carlos helps with deployments.
[00:12] Samir: thanks Alex, we've been excited to talk — we run most of our customer-facing generation on OpenAI currently and some internal experiments on self-hosted vLLM/TGI.
[00:22] Maya: hi all, to add — our goals are lower token costs for customer-facing journeys and being able to guarantee latency for SLAs, especially for some enterprise customers.
[00:34] Priya: great, can you walk me through the current topology? what's on-prem vs cloud, and where do you hit throughput issues?
[00:42] Dan: sure, so production is OpenAI (api) for most flows right now. We have a GPU cluster on-prem that runs vllm for internal ML ops and fine-tuning experiments. The vllm infra is TGI-based for some models — uh, T.G.I — sorry — the hugging face thing.
[01:02] Carlos: when you say vllm, are you using the community vLLM, or a modified runtime? and what GPU types?
[01:09] Dan: community vLLM, mostly A100s in our data center, and some older 80GB cards in cloud. We do 8k and 16k context windows for a few customers.
[01:20] Jules: timeline wise, we have procurement windows in Q3; we want a pilot in July to test parity and a plan to move critical flows by end of year.
[01:30] Alex: ok good, that helps. main themes we usually cover: compatibility (can your prompts / evals run same outputs), latency & cost, and security controls for private deployments. any hard blockers?
[01:42] Maya: data residency and KMS integration — must be able to bring our own keys for encryption in flight and at rest. Also SSO (SAML) for console access.
[01:52] Priya: Redwood Private supports customer KMS and SSO; we also have a private control plane option so your secrets stay in your VPC. We'll share the security whitepaper after.
[02:04] Samir: curious about model compatibility — we rely on the OpenAI APIs for chat completions and function-calling right now. If we move to Redwood hosted or dedicated, how much refactor is required?
[02:16] Priya: for the typical cases we have SDKs and API compat layers; for function-calling we support structured outputs and tool calls, but there are nuance differences in tokenization and some sampling defaults. We usually recommend running an eval parity test using your canonical prompt set.
[02:32] Maya: parity test — what's involved? we have a bench of ~200 prompts including long contexts, instruction-following, and legal redaction tasks.
[02:41] Carlos: perfect — we can run an A/B with OpenAI and Redwood variants, measure top-line metrics: token-cost delta, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), and semantic parity scores. We'll export diffs. Any special prompts that exercise the kv cache or prefix caching?
[02:56] Dan: yes, we use session caching heavily for conversational sessions — we have a prefix cache where we replay system messages. We call it KV cash sometimes (laughs). Concern is that switching runtimes could alter generation due to cache handling.
[03:08] Priya: that's a good callout. Redwood's runtime preserves KV semantics but caching heuristics differ; we'll include the same session reconstruction approach in the eval harness.
[03:18] Samir: performance: our SLO is p95 < 250ms for single-turn queries up to 512 tokens for small-gen flows. Can Redwood meet that on Hosted? On Dedicated?
[03:30] Alex: depends on model and config. On Hosted with smaller/faster models and continuous batching disabled for latency-sensitive endpoints we commonly hit sub-200ms p95 for 512 tokens on our dedicated pools; hosted shared capacity has more variance. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated pools or Private with reserved capacity.
[03:46] Maya: are there quantized model options we can try? 4-bit or 8-bit? we need cost saving without major quality regressions.
[03:54] Priya: yes — we offer quantized variants and quality profiles. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization per workload; we can run the eval harness with FP16, 8-bit, and 4-bit profiles and show delta on the eval set. Expect some degradation on instruction following at 4-bit for some models, but many workloads are fine.
[04:12] Jules: one of our concerns is the model ecosystem — we use GPT-style flavors from OpenAI and Claude for some tasks. If we run open models on Redwood, will there be parity?
[04:23] Carlos: we'll compare model family outputs. Sometimes you won't get 1:1 parity because models differ; the goal is functional parity — same user-visible behavior. For things that must match token-for-token we can run a versioned approach and keep a fallback route to OpenAI for critical flows.
[04:40] Samir: fallback routes — how transparent is routing? can we route by customer, route by latency, or fall back when a model variant drops below quality?
[04:49] Priya: yes, the routing policy supports rules: by latency threshold, error rates, region, or even A/B buckets. We can configure automatic fallback to a host you specify (e.g., OpenAI) when errors spike.
[05:00] Dan: security and audit — we need full request/response logs for diagnostics but must redact PII. How long can logs be retained and can we ship them to our SIEM?
[05:10] Alex: Redis: we have token-level trace retention options; for Private you control retention and can forward logs to your SIEM. We also support encrypted audit logs and can integrate with Syslog/CloudWatch. We'll send the exact retention options in the security pack.
[05:22] Maya: compliance — SOC 2 is table stakes for us. Do you have SOC2+ISO checks?
[05:27] Priya: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II and we have ISO assessments ongoing; for Private deployments we provide harder guarantees and audit support.
[05:34] Samir: ok good. Pricing — we currently pay per-token on OpenAI. We need a predictable cost for Q4 budget asks. How does Dedicated commit pricing work?
[05:44] Alex: Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly/annual commits. We provide a cost model showing per-token cost for your workload (taking batching and cache hit rates into account). We'll run a cost projection based on your traffic shapes.
[05:57] Jules: POC scope — what's a reasonable pilot? We want to test: 1) eval parity on our 200 prompt set, 2) latency SLOs on p95/p99, 3) a small dedicated pool for a week to measure throughput and costs.
[06:10] Carlos: that's doable. Typical pilot is 2-3 weeks: first week run A/B evals; second week spin a small dedicated pod and hit production traffic or replay traffic. We can also do a canary route.
[06:22] Maya: any gotchas migrating from OpenAI function-calling? some of our clients rely on structured tool outputs.
[06:29] Priya: Redwood supports structured output and tool calls; differences are mostly in the return schema enforcement and sampling defaults. For strict schemas we recommend using the structured output validator and supply examples in the prompt. We'll include sample snippets in the migration guide.
[06:45] Samir: about model weights — for Private we host the model images. Are we allowed to bring our own model artifacts? licensing concerns?
[06:54] Alex: yes, you can ship your own model files for Private; licensing needs to be compatible with the models. For dedicated hosted we can also host customer-provided weights behind your tenant with appropriate legal guardrails.
[07:04] Dan: what about on-prem network egress? we want a private control plane but local data flow. Is it air-gapped?
[07:12] Carlos: we offer both: private control plane with VPC peering and an air-gapped on-prem option for regulated workloads. Air-gapped has additional setup and a longer lead time.
[07:22] Maya: performance debugging — do you expose token-by-token traces or KVS?
[07:27] Priya: we expose token traces, KV cache stats, and latency heatmaps per request in the Console. You can also pull raw traces via API for offline analysis.
[07:36] Samir: down the road, can we do model rollbacks and incremental rollouts per customer?
[07:40] Alex: yes, rollouts, canary, A/B and auto-fallbacks are built into the Console.
[07:46] Jules: procurement question — what's the typical lead time for a Dedicated pool?
[07:50] Alex: for Dedicated reserved capacity it's usually 2-6 weeks depending on region and capacity; Private on-prem or air-gapped can take longer. We'll flag exact timelines for your preferred region.
[07:59] Maya: let's talk technical specifics — tokenization differences. We saw drift when switching runtimes, especially around punctuation and tokenizer variants.
[08:08] Priya: tokenization drift is a common source. For parity we recommend freezing tokenizer version in the eval harness and shipping tokenized inputs for a deterministic comparison.
[08:18] Dan: in our vLLM setup we used a custom tokenizer mapping to match OpenAI encodings; would Redwood accept pre-tokenized inputs?
[08:25] Carlos: yes, APIs accept pre-tokenized payloads and we can replay token sequences. That helps when you need deterministic comparisons.
[08:32] Samir: sample rates — how does batching affect latency for low-QPS endpoints? we can't have requests sit in a batch for 30ms+ when low traffic.
[08:41] Priya: the runtime supports continuous batching and can disable or tune batching thresholds for specific routes. For low-QPS critical endpoints we set batch size = 1 or low max latency thresholds.
[08:52] Maya: about eval metrics — we use semantic similarity and human eval. Can Redwood run human-in-the-loop scoring or do we need to supply labels?
[08:59] Carlos: we can orchestrate human eval workflows or accept your labels. For pilot we usually run automated semantic metrics and surface a small human review sample.
[09:09] Samir: curious about Canary rollback triggers — are they automatic if quality drops by X%?
[09:14] Priya: yes, you can define thresholds. e.g., if semantic parity drops by >5% on a rolling window or if p99 latency breaches X, we can automatically rollback and notify.
[09:25] Alex: ok let's capture next steps and owners.
[09:30] (brief cross talk)
[09:34] Maya: quick question — do you support session-level encryption with customer KMS for memory caches?
[09:40] Priya: yes, we support envelope encryption and integrate with customer KMS for key management; memory KV caches can be encrypted at rest and in transit inside the cluster.
[09:49] Dan: one more — can we get a sandbox with dedicated GPUs to replay our production logs? not a huge env, just enough to validate p95 and p99.
[09:57] Carlos: yes, we can provision a small dedicated pod for replay. We'll need sample logs and an access window.
[10:03] Samir: great. any competitor mentions we should call out? we're also evaluating continuation with OpenAI, Anthropic, and a managed partner that does TGI hosting.
[10:12] Alex: noted. We'll include a competitive appendix that outlines differences around routing, dedicated pools, and private deployment timeframes.
[10:19] Priya: summary of what we'll deliver for the pilot: 1) eval parity A/B results on 200 prompts, 2) a small dedicated pod for 1 week for replay, 3) cost projection, 4) security pack and SAML/KMS onboarding doc.
[10:34] Jules: that works. can you also provide a rough pricing ballpark before we engage legal?
[10:39] Alex: yes, we'll send a ballpark and the formal quote after the pilot scope confirms.
[10:46] (closing statements)
[10:50] Maya: ok thanks all — we'll share the prompt set and a sample of logs by EOD tomorrow.
[10:56] Alex: perfect, we'll follow up with action items and schedule the kickoff for the pilot next week.
[11:02] End of recording.

Notes about transcription: speaker attributions may be off in a few places; occasional words like "KV cash" (should be KV cache), "vllm" sometimes capitalized inconsistently, "T.G.I" instead of TGI.
summary: Discovery focused on migrating Ember AI from OpenAI + self-hosted vLLM/TGI to Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private. Main asks: eval parity with 200 prompts, latency SLOs (p95 <250ms), KMS/SSO integration, dedicated pilot for cost/throughput validation, and timelines for Dedicated/Private deployments.
topics: eval parity testing and A/B harness
Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private tradeoffs
KMS and SSO (SAML) for Private deployments
